headline: This new sports app is designed specifically for women’s sports
author: Lauren Forristal

paragraphs.text: A new sports app is looking to change the way fans engage with women’s sports, and it’s doing so without the real-money gambling that has become increasingly common in the sports world.
Called Rival, the app officially launched last weekend on the App Store and Google Play Store, timed to coincide with the National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) Championship.

With Rival, users can make free-to-play picks, earn points, compete on leaderboards, create and join groups, and connect with other fans. The platform also serves as a hub for discovering women’s sports, bringing together schedules, scores, news, highlights, and information on where to watch.

The app is the brainchild of Kelly DiPaola, whose previous experience includes working for Barbra Streisand and producing unscripted television, including Netflix’s “Selling Sunset.” The idea grew out of her frustration with traditional sports apps, which tend to prioritize scores and statistics over the fan experience. Rather than simply creating another place to check game results, DiPaola envisioned a destination dedicated to women’s sports, where fans could build connections, find community, and feel more invested in the games they follow.

“I’m a passionate sports fan, and my partner, Jodie Taylor, is a former England Lioness and now Technical Director at Arsenal Women,” DiPaola told TechCrunch in an email. “The original spark was my frustration with the disparity in women’s sports coverage on traditional sports betting platforms. I’ve never been particularly good at accepting inequality as the status quo, so I decided to do something about it.”

That vision comes at a time when women’s sports are experiencing record growth in attendance and viewership. Yet greater visibility doesn’t necessarily translate into a better experience for fans, particularly women who participate in mainstream sports communities online.
Platforms such as Reddit, X, and sports-focused forums can expose women — especially women of color and LGBTQ+ athletes — to harassment, abuse, and discriminatory commentary.

The problem is well documented. A 2024 NCAA study found that online abuse targeting student-athletes peaked during March Madness, with women’s basketball players receiving three times as many threats as their male counterparts.

Rival is positioning itself as an alternative to that experience, placing positive social connection and community at the center of its platform. Users can create profiles and statuses, follow other users, and create or join groups around their favorite teams and sports.

“Women’s sports doesn’t just have a visibility problem. It has a participation problem,” DiPaola said. “I wanted to build somewhere that felt like walking into your favorite local bar on a Friday night, where you could turn up on your own and still feel like you belonged, like you were part of something bigger than yourself.”

Although the app is focused on women’s teams and competitions, anyone can join. The platform also includes blocking and reporting tools, private profiles, private groups, in-app support, and moderation features designed to address abusive behavior.

“Our responsibility is to create a safe and welcoming environment for everyone,” DiPaola said. “We have zero tolerance for abuse, harassment, or discrimination, and accounts engaging in such behavior are subject to removal. As our community grows, our moderation capabilities will need to grow with it.”

Another major differentiator is Rival’s decision to avoid real-money sports betting altogether. Instead, the platform centers on what the company describes as “friendly competition,” allowing users to make predictions and compete with friends without putting money on the line.

That distinction is particularly timely as sports betting continues to expand across the U.S., raising concerns about its consequences. According to the American Gaming Association, Americans wagered $166.94 billion on legal sports betting last year. A UCLA study found that, in states allowing online sports gambling, the likelihood of a personal bankruptcy filing increased by around 25%.

At launch, Rival covers 36 leagues and competitions, 1,979 teams, and more than 20,000 athletes internationally. This includes NCAA Women’s Basketball, NCAA Softball, Women’s Professional Football League, EuroLeague, and more.

DiPaola says the company ultimately wants to represent every sport women play, including those that have historically received less coverage. That will mean exploring partnerships to improve data availability for underrepresented sports and leagues.

Looking ahead, Rival also plans to expand its sports coverage, develop its live-picks ecosystem, introduce “richer” social and community features, and bring fan participation closer to live broadcasts.
